reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it demonstrates an ordinary Target shopping promotion involving household products, manufacturer coupons, and a store coupon. The speaker explains how the coupons reduce a purchase from $50.20 to $11.60, with the receipt showing product, coupon, tax, and gift-card entries. The text-message instruction is presented as a way to obtain the Target coupon, but the available video evidence notes that the number or wording may be incorrect and does not establish any external service behavior or outcome.

citations.quote: I love the 15 off 50 household when they do that deal.
make sure you have the 15 off of 50 household coupon
My total came to $50.20 before the coupon. After coupons it dropped down to $11.60.
And I used a gift card, I paid nothing out of pocket.
if you do not have the gift card you'll just pay $11.60 and whatever your tax is

opening.argument: Judge, consider the promise alongside the action requested. The video presents the purchase as free after coupons and gift cards, then tells viewers to obtain the household coupon by text and have it scanned from their phones. That is a concrete participation path tied to the free-purchase claim. The speaker's own accounting shows why the distinction matters: the coupons did not make the goods free; gift cards covered the remaining amount. A viewer drawn in by the free claim is still being steered to assemble coupons and make a purchase.

After coupons it dropped down to $11.60. $2.67 was my tax. $14.27 after tax, and after coupons, and the category coupon. And I used a gift card, I paid nothing out of pocket.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense's $11.60 figure confirms that coupons alone do not deliver the advertised free purchase. Saying the text instruction merely obtains a coupon does not separate it from the pitch: viewers are told to use the phone coupon as part of duplicating the deal. Nor does uncertainty about the typed number settle the concern; the description supplies a text instruction while acknowledging a possible error in the video.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The title expressly qualifies “FREE” with “after coupons & gift cards.” The speaker discloses both the post-coupon cost and the role of gift cards, including what someone without one would pay. The text step is an offered way to obtain a household coupon, not evidence of a separate reward claim or deceptive claim process.

opening.argument: Judge, the combination of signals deserves scrutiny: a headline calling the purchase free, a time-limited deal, a text-message route to the coupon, and a gift-card payment that makes the out-of-pocket result sound effortless. The speaker also acknowledges uncertainty about the text instruction and says the Febreze coupon took off less than expected. These details do not prove the text route is harmful, but they do make the confident free-purchase presentation less reliable than it first sounds. The demonstrated result depends on conditions that a viewer may not reproduce.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats the receipt as settling the issue, but the receipt supports one transaction, not the repeated suggestion that others can duplicate the result. The speaker herself reports a coupon taking off less than expected, and her zero out-of-pocket payment required gift cards. The defense is right that no external text-service outcome is established; that limits what can be claimed about the text route, but it does not erase its role in the pitch.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Those details are disclosed qualifications, not hidden conditions. The speaker identifies the coupon discrepancy, states the amount due after coupons, and explains that gift cards covered it. She even gives the cost for viewers without gift cards. Neither a deadline nor a corrected text instruction establishes that the ordinary household offer is deceptive.

opening.argument: Judge, this is more than a retrospective account of a shopping trip. The speaker says she chose the products so others could duplicate the deal, tells viewers to secure the household coupon, and walks them through what to present at checkout. The title leads with a free-purchase outcome. Taken together, the demonstration functions as an invitation to pursue that outcome, even though the speaker's own figures show a remaining charge after coupons. The instructional format should not obscure the promotional force of the free claim.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense accurately describes the mechanics, but detailed mechanics can also make a solicitation more persuasive. Here, the speaker explicitly designs the purchase for others to repeat and instructs them at checkout. Showing a receipt supports what happened in her transaction; it does not turn the invitation to pursue a free result into a purely neutral report. The gift-card qualification is real, but it is also indispensable to the headline's outcome.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: An instruction to repeat a purchase does not by itself make it a scam solicitation. The speaker describes ordinary store and manufacturer coupons, checks whether app coupons attach, and openly distinguishes the discounted price from paying with gift cards. The title makes that gift-card condition explicit. The promotional reading identifies an invitation to shop, but not a deceptive reward or claim flow.
